new_statements.translation: Pronunciation of Mbamba and Umbangala. The vowels as in Italian, almost as in German. [...] The accent usually falls on the penultimate syllable. — [p.137:] Ba- and Ci-, pl. I-, are just prefixes and the final -la in Imbangala is probably only a suffix, for I have often heard the accent on the second syllable (Imbángala).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent normally on the penultimate syllable (stated jointly for Chatelain's Mbamba and Umbangala material); 'gewöhnlich' signals unstated exceptions, one of which he notes himself: the ethnonym Imbángala with accent on the antepenult/second syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the hedge 'gewöhnlich' (usually) and the observed Imbángala (accent on second syllable of a four-syllable word, i.e. not penult), which he explains morphologically (-la a suffix).
new_statements.domain_note: Impressionistic 19th-century note on isolated words elicited from one Imbangala speaker (a woman from Kasanji living in Malanji) plus Mbamba speakers; word-level citation forms; no discussion of tone (the language is Bantu and presumably tonal, which the source does not address).
new_statements.identity_note: Chatelain's 'Umbangala' is the speech of the Imbangala (Ci-mbangala) of Kasanji/Cassange, Malanje - i.e. Nuclear Mbangala [nucl1380] under mban1264; nothing found for the Yongo dialect [yong1279]. The accent sentence is given jointly for 'Mbamba und Umbangala'; his Mbamba is the lect of Soba Mbangu's village near Malanji (a Kimbundu-area/Hungu-affiliated variety, not Mbangala), so the statement is shared rather than Mbangala-specific. Glottolog's Weeks 1910 and Barney 1934 refs under mban1264 concern Bangala of the Upper Congo (bang1353 area), not this language; Tubomeshi 1966 describes 'Minungu', whose identity with H34 is unverified.

new_statements.quote: The stress mark is ¯, and the unstress ˘. Neither is employed unless the pronunciation of the vowel is exceptionally deep or light. The accent or pitch of the voice is indicated by ´. This is so normally and frequently on the penultimate syllable that the accent is only employed when an exception to the prevailing rule in Bantu transfers the voice-pitch to the first, last, or other syllable than the penultimate. Monosyllables are not accented unless uttered with vehemence. [p. 41] — [p. 804:] 114. UMBANGALA or IMBÁNGŒLA, 114 a. YOÑGŒ. This language of the Upper Kwañgo river, in the district of Kasanji, is chiefly made known to us by a short vocabulary published by Héli Chatelain in the Zeits. f. afr. Spr., Berlin, 1889

Neither is employed unless the pronunciation of the vowel is exceptionally deep or light. The accent or pitch of the voice is indicated by acute. This is so normally and frequently on the penultimate syllable that the accent is only employed when an exception to the prevailing rule in Bantu transfers the voice-pitch to the first, last, or other syllable than the penultimate. Monosyllables are not accented unless uttered with vehemence.' is verbatim on the page (the scanned text). Opened printed p. 804): heading '114. UMBANGALA or IMBANGWLA, 114a. YONGW.' with a clear acute on the A of the second syllable…
new_statements.relation_note: Consistent with the catalog's penultimate rule, but only as the general Bantu default of Johnston's transcription applied to unmarked Umbangala vocabulary; the marked ethnonym Imbáng(w)ala reproduces Chatelain's second-syllable exception. Not an independent language-specific statement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A Bantu-wide convention, not an Umbangala-specific statement: accent/pitch falls on the penultimate syllable by default, and Johnston marks it only where it falls elsewhere. The Umbangala column (no. 114, pp. 411–426; p. 411 checked on the image: Ñ-gimbŭ, Ki-ama, Lun-jinji, Ka-sumuna, Ku-aku, Ka-legela, Mu-fula, Li-kwa) carries no accent marks, so under his convention every listed Umbangala word is penultimate. The one marked form is the ethnonym in the §114 heading, IMBÁNGŒLA (acute on the second syllable), i.e. a non-penult exception on the name, the same exception Chatelain 1889 noted ('Imbángala'). The §114 paragraph itself is bibliographic (Chatelain 1889, 1894; = Koelle's 'Kasandsh'; Yoñgŏ a northern dialect).
new_statements.exceptions: General: accent marked only when it falls on the first, last or other non-penult syllable; monosyllables unaccented unless uttered with vehemence. For Umbangala specifically only the ethnonym Imbáng(w)ala is marked non-penult.
new_statements.identity_note: Chatelain's Umbangala (the catalog's source) was collected from a Kasanji woman in Malanje and is the speech of the Imbangala of Kasanje (Upper Kwango). Johnston's no. 114 'Umbangala or Imbangala' is the same variety (Upper Kwango, district of Kasanji; equated with Koelle's 'Kasandsh'; Yongo a northern dialect). Maia's dictionary describes Kimbundu (kimb1241) and Kikongo, not Umbangala. Weeks 1910 and Barney 1934 concern the Bangala of the Upper Congo River (DR Congo, Lingala area), a different language attached to mban1264 by name only.
